newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South African business urges govt to seek IMF support.
newsitem.headline: South African business urges govt to seek IMF support.

text.p: The South African Chamber of Business (Sacob) said on Tuesday the government should seek International Monetary Fund (IMF) assistance to stabilise the ailing rand and restore investor confidence.
Ben van Rensburg, Sacob's director of economic policy, said there were widespread fears that a destabilisation in the rand would lead to a destabilisation of the whole economy.
"The government must bring the IMF into the picture," van Rensburg said at a presentation of Sacob's monthly business confidence index, which in October plunged to a 14-month low.
"When we experience a balance of payments (BOP) problem we must be able to make use of the IMF's standby facility...We need to let speculators (on the rand) know we are not on our own."
The rand has lost over 30 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar since the middle of February, sinking to its weakest levels ever last week.
Alongside IMF support, government also needed to provide a clear timetable on the abolition of exchange controls, van Rensburg said.
"On the lifting of exchange controls we need a clear cut programme and to show we are moving towards this," he said.

Earlier on Tuesday Finance Minister Trevor Manuel told reporters in Cape Town no final deadline had been set for abolition of exchange controls. He also said South Africa might in future retain a "modicum" of foreign exchange controls.
On IMF support, Manuel said although a standy facility remained an option, the government was not currently in discussion with the organisation who he said would remain a lender of last resort.

Sacob director-general Raymond Parsons urged government to initiate IMF talks, and not to let vociferous opposition to the IMF from some left-wing members of the ruling African National Congress (ANC) stand in its way.
"We need to put aside preconceived notions of the IMF and talk to them from a position of strength," Parsons said.
Under IMF rules, South Africa would be able to draw up to 100 percent of its IMF quota -- or some $2 billion -- for use as a standby or extended fund facility.
IMF managing director Michel Camdessus said last month that the institution was prepared to support South Africa's reserves and provide funding, if asked.
But many in the ANC are wary of the stigma attached to IMF aid, following unpopular IMF interventions elsewhere in Africa.
